Why open access pays for itself: the netting mechanism

If open access lets customers leave, why choose it? Because a CCP's product gets better as it gets bigger. Netting means offsetting a bank's bought and sold positions in the same product so it only posts margin on the difference. Initial margin (IM) is the collateral a member posts up front to cover losses if it fails. The more trades from more venues that sit in one CCP, the more of them cancel out, and the less margin each bank has to post. Figure 20 shows the mechanism with invented numbers.

Two real numbers show this at work. SwapClear holds over 90% of cleared interest rate swap notional outstanding, by LSEG's own claim [S303], and in 2023 it compressed 7.8 million trades [S356]. Compression means tearing up offsetting trades and replacing them with fewer, smaller ones that carry the same risk. A pool that big is hard for a rival to match, which is why open access gives LCH more than it takes away. Inferred

Say this in the interview

"LSEG is built as separate regulated businesses partly because regulators require it, but mainly because LCH's value depends on being neutral. Its articles say no exchange will be favoured, so trades come in from rival venues and bilateral deals as well as LSEG's own. More trades in one pool means more netting and less margin for everyone, which is why SwapClear holds over 90% of cleared swaps. The cost is real: Euronext could take its clearing away, and it did."

Don't say this

"LSEG is an integrated exchange that keeps trading and clearing in-house." That describes Deutsche Börse's model, not LSEG's. Also avoid "LCH is 82.6% owned": the current figure is about 94% [S300, S121].

Your opinion goes here

Prompt: Was the £1.2bn paid to SwapClear's founding banks worth it? For: it lifted group EBITDA margin by 100bps at once [S72] and locked the banks in until 2045. Against: the banks still take 10% for 20 years, and the cash could have funded buybacks. Suggested position: worth it, because it bought both margin and loyalty in the business with the deepest moat; but say you would want to see how the 10% share is measured and reviewed.

MK1040KMQ2. How the businesses work together

LSEG's language here is precise, and you should match it. Its Code of Conduct defines the value Partnership as: "Our open model is integral to how we do business. We forge long-term relationships; we work together to solve evolving needs and deliver strategic outcomes" [S307]. The 2025 Annual Report heads its integration section "Monetising our integrated business" [S300]. Note what these phrases claim: an open model, and an integrated offering to customers. They do not claim that trading and clearing are tied together.

Why this matters

The pattern is clear: LSEG's businesses meet through data, distribution, technology and account management. They do not meet through clearing favours. That is the line the law draws (Figure 21), and it is what lets LSEG say "open model" and "integrated offering" in the same breath. Inferred

Where they deliberately do not work together

  • No clearing favours. LCH must not favour LSEG venues or their users [S305].
  • Information barriers. The OFT required "conflict of interest provisions and information barriers" so that rival venues could talk to LCH "assured of the confidentiality of those discussions from LSEG" [S305].
  • A listed subsidiary with its own board. Tradeweb has its own share price, buybacks and board, and 49.1% of its economics belong to others [S300, S137]. Group decisions must respect Tradeweb's public shareholders. Inferred
  • Client confidentiality. The FX Global Code requires firms to "clearly and effectively identify and appropriately limit access to Confidential Information" (Principle 19) [S343], and LSEG's Code says staff "must never disclose confidential information... unless there is a legitimate need to know" [S307].
Don't say this

"LSEG bundles SwapClear clearing with Tradeweb swaps trading", or "ForexClear is sold together with FXall". No LSEG statement ties these pairs commercially, and the open-access clause makes it unlikely [S305]. If you want to show you know the links, use RepoAgent, FTSE Russell pricing off Tradeweb, or FXall inside Workspace instead.

Say this in the interview

"The businesses meet through data, distribution and technology rather than through clearing. RepoAgent is the clearest joint product: Post Trade Solutions and Tradeweb built it together to reduce repo settlement fails. And LSEG says a large proportion of FXall's functionality is now inside Workspace. I'd be curious how the FX team measures whether clients actually move their workflow across."

What they buy, and why they accept the fees

Customers do not buy "infrastructure". They buy six concrete things, each of which saves them money, capital or risk that they would otherwise carry. Figure 22 maps them.

1. Default protection that has been tested

When Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008, SwapClear held a "$9 trillion OTC portfolio" of "over 66,000 trades", backed by "$2 billion" of Lehman's initial margin. LCH used "only 35% of its initial margin", ran five currency auctions and had all positions dealt with by week three [S354]. No default fund money was used [S354, S355]. LCH says it has "managed 9 member defaults and, in all cases, losses were within the initial margin held" [S351]. Confirmed Part 2 explains the default waterfall that sits behind this.

Key term

Default fund and waterfall: if a member fails, its own margin and default fund contribution are used first, then LCH's own capital ("skin in the game"), then other members' default fund contributions [S351]. Lehman never got past the first step.

2. Netting and compression free up capital

See Figure 20. LCH charges fees for compression, and OTC Derivatives revenue rose 11.6% in 2025 "driven by growth in clearing and compression activity" [S301, S304]. 7.8 million SwapClear trades were compressed in 2023 [S356]; a 2025 figure was not found.

3. Margin efficiency

LCH sets initial margin at "an enhanced 99.7% confidence interval" [S351], which means the margin should cover losses on all but about 3 days in 1,000. ForexClear uses "historical simulation expected shortfall... ten years of historical market data" [S352]. Customers can post bonds rather than cash: average non-cash collateral was €209.6bn against €101.3bn of cash in 2025 [S301]. Cash tied up in margin earns little, so being able to post bonds instead is worth money to the customer. Inferred

4. Liquidity in one place

SwapClear has over 90% of cleared interest rate swap notional outstanding [S303]. It cleared $1,941 trillion of notional in 2025 and a record 13.4 million trades [S301, S304]. Tradeweb's average daily volume (ADV) was $2.6 trillion in 2025 and $3.2 trillion in H1 2026 [S301, S302]. Liquidity attracts liquidity: a buyer goes where most sellers already are.

5. Data accuracy

"Data quality issues raised by customers have fallen 51% despite total content volumes rising 113%" over four years [S301]. For a bank, a wrong price in a risk model is a regulatory and financial problem, so accuracy is part of what it pays for.

6. Access to capital

Debt issuers use LSE's markets to raise money from professional investors, with LSEG's own figure of 1,300 borrowers raising $500 to $600bn a year [S316]. Part 6 covers the primary markets process. Reported

Part 4

How LSEG stands out

LSEG is not the biggest, fastest-growing or leanest exchange group, but it is the only one that combines a global swaps clearing utility, terminal-scale data, a global index house and multi-asset venues under one roof.

MK1044KMHow to use this part

"Why LSEG and not ICE or CME?" and "Who are our competitors?" are standard interview questions. A weak answer lists firms. A strong answer says which business line competes with whom, on what measure, with a number, and admits where LSEG is behind. This part gives you the comparison tables, the design choices that separate the groups, six claims only LSEG can make, the places it does not lead, and a line-by-line competitor map.

Read the numbers with care

Every firm reports in its own currency and defines revenue differently (net revenue, revenue less transaction costs, total income excluding recoveries). The research keeps each number in its home currency [S120]. Where this part converts to US dollars, the rate is the author's round-number assumption (£1 = $1.30, €1 = $1.15), marked Inferred. Say "roughly" when you compare sizes out loud. Market caps are a single aggregator snapshot from October 2026 [S148] Reported.

MK1046KMSize against staffing

Revenue per employee is a rough measure of how labour-heavy a business model is. Exchanges and clearing houses run on automated systems, so a small team can handle huge volumes. Data businesses need people to collect, clean, sell and support content.

Correction: LSEG's headcount

The competitor workstream divided LSEG's income by "c.14,200" people, giving c.£633k per head. That is wrong for a like-for-like comparison: 14,200 (precisely 14,244) is LSEG's engineering headcount, which fell from 15,101 [S300, S120]. The group had 28,516 employees at the end of 2025 [S300]. The table below uses 28,516, which roughly halves LSEG's revenue per head to c.£315k. Inferred If an interviewer has seen the £633k figure, you can explain the difference.

Two points to take from this. First, LSEG is people-heavy, and you should say so plainly: at about £315k per head it sits below every venue operator and below ICE, Nasdaq and MSCI, and only roughly level with S&P Global and Deutsche Börse once currencies are converted. The reason is the work: data collection and cleaning, customer support, operations and engineering are labour-intensive, and LSEG runs much of that from hubs, with 8,541 employees in India alone [S300]. It is not a lean exchange; it is a data company with a large Markets division. Inferred

Second, inside LSEG the Markets businesses look like the venue cluster: Tradeweb alone earns about $1.3m per head [S137], and Markets runs at a 55.6% EBITDA margin (58.6% in H1 2026) against 40.7% for D&A [S120, S72]. That is why Markets is the group's profit and growth engine. Inferred

MK1047KMFour design choices, and where each rival sits

Exchange groups differ less in what they do than in how they are built. Four design choices separate them. Figure 25 places each firm on each axis; the text below gives the evidence.

Axis 1: transaction-heavy or subscription-heavy revenue

At the transaction end: CME (81% from clearing and transaction fees), Tradeweb (82.8% transaction fees), Cboe [S122, S137, S132]. At the subscription end: MSCI (73% recurring subscriptions), Nasdaq (about 77% Solutions) [S136, S130]. LSEG is near the data end, with about 61% of income from its three subscription divisions; ICE sits in the middle at about 51% recurring [S120, S124]. Why it matters for Markets: the Markets division is LSEG's volume-driven, volatility-sensitive part, and it grew faster (+8.9%) than D&A (+5.0%) in 2025 [S120].

Axis 2: vertical silo or open access clearing

Deutsche Börse calls its model "vertically integrated" [S127]. Euronext pulled cash equity clearing out of LCH SA into its own CCP, which LSEG names as the reason Securities & Reporting revenue fell 3.0% [S120]. LSEG is the open-access end: SwapClear has "over 100 members" and clears 28 currencies [S141]. Watch out: the silo model is gaining in euro swaps, where Eurex rose to 13.5% in Q3 2025 from 8.4% a year earlier [S139] Reported.

Axis 3: exchange-owned or user-partnered clearing

LSEG owns about 94% of LCH [S121, S300], but keeps users inside: founding banks share 10% of SwapClear's revenue surplus until 2045, and 11 banks bought 20% of Post Trade Solutions for £170m [S120]. No comparable bank-equity structure was found at CME, ICE or Eurex clearing Inferred, though this was not checked exhaustively.

Axis 4: strength as a listings venue

London had 23 IPOs raising £2.1bn in 2025, up 170% on £777.7m in 2024 [S142], and 7 IPOs raising £577m in H1 2026 [S143]. Hong Kong raised HK$286.9bn from 119 IPOs, ranked first in the world [S134]; US proceeds rose 38% and led the world by value [S144]. 88 companies left London's main market in 2024 [S145] Reported. This is why listings are a small part of LSEG's revenue and why the JD's research track mentions debt listings.

A fifth difference: the listed subsidiary and the tech partner

LSEG controls Tradeweb with about 89.9% of the votes but only about half the economics [S137, S300]; CME and ICE own their fixed income venues outright [S122, S124]. And LSEG's cloud deal is a product partnership as well as infrastructure: Microsoft owns about 4% of LSEG, LSEG committed to $2.8bn of minimum cloud spend, and Workspace now runs inside Teams and Excel [S147, S120]. CME is moving to Google Cloud [S122].

MK1048KMSix things only LSEG can claim

Each claim below is phrased so that it is true and checkable. "Only" claims are the author's comparison across the peer set in Table A and B, so say "no other exchange group I looked at" rather than "no one in the world". Inferred

1. It runs the world's swaps clearing utility

Evidence

SwapClear cleared a record $1,941 trillion of interest rate swap notional in 2025 (+21.2%) and 5.3 million client trades (+33%) [S120]. Clarus data: 99.995% of GBP SONIA swaps in Q1 2026; CME's best-ever share of USD OIS was only 4.3% [S140]. LSEG says SwapClear clears "95 percent of all 'vanilla' OTC interest rate swap products" [S141] (undated company claim).

Why it matters

Clearing has network effects: offsets improve as more trades sit in one pool (Figure 20). That is a moat built over 25 years. The 2025 surplus deal with founding banks added 100bps to group EBITDA margin [S120].

2. One group owns terminal-scale data, a global index house, multi-asset venues and a global CCP

Evidence

D&A £3,978m, FTSE Russell £954m, plus Tradeweb, FXall and FX Matching, LSE, Turquoise and LCH [S120]. ICE has data, exchanges and clearing but no FX venue or desktop of this scale; Deutsche Börse has 360T, Eurex and an index business but no terminal; Bloomberg has a terminal, FXGO and bond trading but no CCP or exchange. Inferred

Why it matters

It is the basis for cross-selling and for distributing data everywhere customers work: "The combination of our trade lifecycle and data value chains is unmatched" [S303].

3. A bank-partnership model built into its infrastructure

Evidence

Banks share 10% of the SwapClear revenue surplus until 2045 and own 20% of Post Trade Solutions [S120]; clearing members and clients sit on LCH's risk committee, with no constituent holding a majority [S304]. No comparable structure found at CME, ICE or Deutsche Börse clearing Inferred.

Why it matters

Banks are 72% of LSEG's income [S303]. Giving them a seat and a share makes them less likely to back a rival CCP, as they once did when founding Turquoise and Tradeweb.

4. A controlled, separately listed subsidiary worth over $20bn

Evidence

Tradeweb: revenue $2,052m (+18.9%), ADV $2.6trn, market cap $22.28bn [S137, S120, S148]. LSEG holds about 89.9% of votes and 50.9% of the economics [S137, S300]. No other exchange group in the peer set consolidates a listed company of that size. Inferred

Why it matters

Tradeweb is the fastest-growing big piece of Markets, but about half of its profit belongs to outside shareholders, and it has its own board. Coordinating with it (RepoAgent, Workspace integration) is a live business management task [S301, S302].

5. Microsoft as shareholder and product partner

Evidence

About 4% stake, 10-year term, $2.8bn minimum cloud spend [S147]; Workspace in Teams, Excel and PowerPoint add-ins, Autex on Azure, data on Microsoft Fabric [S120]; AI data partnerships with Anthropic, Databricks, Microsoft, OpenAI, Rogo and Snowflake [S120].

Why it matters

It puts LSEG's data inside the tools customers already use, which is LSEG's answer to the fear that AI tools will bypass terminals. Some investors see the rollout as slower than promised (see Part 2).

6. FX across the whole workflow

Evidence

FXall (dealer-to-client) plus FX Matching (dealer-to-dealer): $525bn average daily volume in 2025; ForexClear cleared $48,113bn notional, up 31.4% [S120]. Deutsche Börse (360T) and Cboe FX lack an interbank matching platform of this scale plus FX clearing in the same group; CME has EBS but no dealer-to-client platform like FXall. Inferred

Why it matters

The FX customer track in the JD sits here. A client can trade, confirm and clear FX within LSEG businesses, but each step is still a separate service under open access.

Don't say this

"LSEG is the oldest exchange in the world" or other history claims that the competitor research did not verify. And do not say Tradeweb is wholly owned: it is majority-owned and separately listed [S137].

MK1005KM
Part 5

The industry from zero

What financial market infrastructure is, how money moves through it, who pays for it, and the forces that will reshape it while you are at LSEG.

This Part assumes you know nothing about how markets are wired together. By the end you should be able to do three things in an interview: walk through a trade from start to finish and name the LSEG business at each step, explain how an exchange group makes money (and why it is mostly not from the stock exchange), and give a reasoned view on where the industry goes in the next three to five years.

Why this matters

The JD asks for people who "want to understand the full breadth of our organisation, how it fits together, how it functions". That is a direct request for this Part. The candidate who can say "LSE is the execution step, LCH is the clearing step, and the prices from both are resold by Data & Analytics" sounds like someone already inside the firm. Inferred

MK1051KMWhat financial market infrastructure is

Think of a financial market as a giant marketplace. The traders (banks, fund managers, hedge funds) are the shoppers and stallholders. Financial market infrastructure is the plumbing that lets them deal safely: the shops, the tills, the receipts and the delivery vans. FMIs do not usually take bets themselves. They make it possible for others to trade, and they charge a toll for doing so. Inferred

Key term

FMI (financial market infrastructure): the shared systems that let financial trades happen and complete: trading venues, clearing houses, settlement systems, trade repositories, plus (in a wider sense) the index and data businesses that sit around them. LSEG calls itself a financial markets infrastructure and data group, not an exchange.

Source uncertain

The "plumbing" analogy and the one-line definitions in the table below come from the WS4 research summary, which marks several of them as general knowledge (OTF, CSD, UnaVista). They are standard textbook definitions, but treat the LSEG examples for CSD and trade repository as Inferred rather than confirmed.

Eight kinds of FMI, in one table

TypeWhat it does, in one lineLSEG exampleMain competitors
Exchange (in law a "regulated market", RM)A rule-based place where securities are admitted (listed) and traded, under the strictest rules.London Stock Exchange Main MarketEuronext, Deutsche Börse, Nasdaq, NYSE (ICE)
MTF (multilateral trading facility)A venue that brings many buyers and sellers together under fixed, non-discretionary rules, with lighter regulation than an exchange.Turquoise; AIM and the International Securities Market (ISM) are MTFs run by LSE [S176]Cboe Europe, Aquis
OTF (organised trading facility)A venue for bonds and derivatives where the operator has some discretion over how orders meet. InferredNot a focus hereInterdealer brokers
CCP (central counterparty, clearing house)Steps into the middle of a trade: buyer to every seller, seller to every buyer. Collects margin so that if one side fails, the other still gets paid.LCH (LCH Ltd, London; LCH SA, Paris): SwapClear, ForexClear, RepoClear, CDSClearCME Clearing, Eurex Clearing, ICE Clear
CSD (central securities depository)Keeps the official record of who owns which securities and moves them from seller to buyer at settlement.Not LSEG's main UK business: the UK CSD is Euroclear UK & International InferredEuroclear, Clearstream

Key term

Regulated market vs MTF: both are trading venues. A regulated market is the "full" exchange, where admission brings the heaviest disclosure rules (for example a prospectus). An MTF is lighter. That is why LSE runs its Main Market as a regulated market but AIM (for growth companies) and ISM (for professional-only bonds) as MTFs [S176].

Key term

Clearing house (CCP): after a trade is agreed, the CCP becomes the counterparty to both sides. It holds margin (collateral each member posts) and a default fund (a shared pot members pay into) so one firm's failure does not spread. Not a bank: it mutualises risk rather than lending.

The point to carry into interview. Most firms in this table do one or two of these jobs. LSEG does five at once: exchange (LSE), MTF (Turquoise, AIM, ISM), CCP (LCH), index provider (FTSE Russell) and data vendor (Data & Analytics). That "vertical" mix is why it describes itself as an infrastructure and data group rather than a stock exchange. Inferred The competitor research backs this up: ICE has data, exchanges and clearing but no FX venue or desktop of LSEG's scale; Deutsche Börse has 360T, Eurex and an index arm but no terminal; Bloomberg has a terminal, FXGO and bond trading but no CCP or exchange [S120]. Inferred

MK1052KMThe trade lifecycle, step by step

Every trade, whether a share, a bond, a swap or a currency, goes through the same five steps. Learn them in order. The interviewer question "walk me through what happens when someone buys a share" is really a test of whether you know this chain.

  1. Pre-trade data. Before trading, an investor looks at prices, quotes, news, indices and analytics. Data vendors and venues sell this. (LSEG Data & Analytics, LSE market data, FTSE Russell index levels.)
  2. Execution. The buyer and seller agree a price and size, either on a venue (an exchange, an MTF, an RFQ platform like Tradeweb, an FX platform like FXall) or directly between two parties, which is called over the counter (OTC).
  3. Clearing. The trade is confirmed and, if centrally cleared, a CCP like LCH becomes the counterparty to both sides and collects margin.
  4. Settlement. Cash and securities actually change hands at a CSD, or for FX through a system like CLS. Under the UK's planned T+1 cycle, settlement must happen no later than one business day after the trade, from 11 October 2027 [S158]. Confirmed
  5. Post-trade reporting. Trades are published (transparency) and reported to the regulator or a trade repository. Consolidated tapes pull published trade data from all venues into one feed [S155].
Key term

Netting: offsetting buys against sells so only the net amount needs settling or margining. The more trades sit in one CCP, the more can be netted, which lowers members' margin. This is the network effect behind LCH SwapClear's dominance. Inferred

Key term

T+1: settlement one business day after the trade date ("T"). The UK and EU both plan to move from two days to one on 11 October 2027 [S158, S159]. Less time to fix errors means more automation.

Key term

Settlement risk and PvP: in FX you pay one currency and wait for the other. If the counterparty fails in between, you lose the full amount (also called Herstatt risk). PvP (payment versus payment) settles both legs at once or not at all. CLS, operating since September 2002, is the main PvP system [S204]. About $1.4tn a day of FX still settles with no protection [S205]. Confirmed

Say this in the interview

"If I buy a FTSE 100 share, I probably checked the price on a data screen first, which could be LSEG Data & Analytics. The order executes on the London Stock Exchange order book or on Turquoise. It is cleared by a CCP, settled at the CSD, and the trade price is published and resold as data. LSEG is at four of the five steps; settlement is the one it does not run in the UK. From October 2027 that settlement has to happen in one day, not two."

The JD's own wording maps onto steps 2 to 5: LSEG Markets helps customers "across the trade life cycle, ensuring compliance and efficiency in clearing and reporting obligations, while granting access to diverse liquidity pools". "Liquidity pools" is step 2 (venues), "clearing" is step 3, "reporting obligations" is step 5. Confirmed

MK1053KMFour distinctions interviewers assume you know

These four pairs come up in every markets conversation. Each one decides which LSEG business is involved and how it gets paid.

DistinctionSide ASide BLSEG link
Primary vs secondaryPrimary: new securities are created and sold for the first time to raise money (an IPO, a new bond). The issuer gets the cash.Secondary: existing securities trade between investors. The issuer gets nothing, but a liquid secondary market is why investors buy in the primary market.LSE listing and debt capital markets teams work in primary. LSE, Turquoise, Tradeweb, FXall work in secondary.
Lit vs darkLit: orders are visible to everyone before trading (pre-trade transparency).Dark: orders are hidden until after execution, so big investors can trade without moving the price.Turquoise runs both a lit book and a dark book (Turquoise Plato). Inferred
Order book vs RFQOrder book (CLOB): continuously matches anonymous buy and sell orders by price, then time. How most shares trade.RFQ (request for quote): a client asks a few dealers for a price and picks the best. How most bonds, swaps and much FX trade.LSE is a CLOB; Tradeweb's core model is RFQ. LSE 24 "intends to draw on elements of central limit order book and request-for-quote functionality" [S196]. Confirmed
OTC vs exchange-tradedOTC: negotiated directly between two parties, often a bank and a client (most FX, bonds, swaps).Exchange-traded: standardised products on a venue (shares, futures).After 2008, G20 rules pushed standard OTC derivatives into central clearing, which is why LCH SwapClear is so large. Inferred
Key term

CLOB (central limit order book): a matching engine that lists every bid and offer by price and time and matches them automatically. Anonymous, continuous, good for small standard trades.

Key term

RFQ (request for quote): the client sends a request to, say, five dealers, they reply with prices, the client picks one. Good for large or illiquid trades where nobody wants to show their hand in public.

Key term

Liquidity: how easily you can trade something in size without moving its price. A "liquidity pool" is a place where many buyers and sellers meet. Liquidity attracts liquidity: traders go where other traders are, which is why venues compete hard and why market share is sticky once won. Inferred

Why the order book vs RFQ split matters for the JD. Shares trade mostly on order books, bonds and FX mostly by RFQ or bilateral dealing. Tradeweb (RFQ) contributed £1,539m to LSEG Markets in 2025 under "Fixed Income, Derivatives & Other", far more than the £412m from Equities [S120]. Confirmed So the RFQ world is where most of LSEG's trading income sits, not the famous order book. Inferred

Key term

Buy side and sell side: the sell side is banks and dealers who make prices and sell products. The buy side is investors who buy them: asset managers, pension funds, insurers, hedge funds. NBFI (non-bank financial institution) covers hedge funds, proprietary traders and asset managers outside banking. BCG: "NBFIs are no longer peripheral players, they are central to how capital is being formed, intermediated, and traded" [S186].

Key term

Recurring (subscription) vs transactional revenue: recurring revenue is paid on a contract whether or not markets are busy (data, index licences). Transactional revenue is paid per trade, so it jumps in volatile markets and falls in quiet ones. Investors pay a higher price for recurring revenue because it is predictable. LSEG's CEO in July 2026: "Growth in our subscription businesses is accelerating" [S195]. Confirmed

So what for a Markets intern? You would sit in the transactional part of a mostly subscription group. That is not a weakness. Markets grew faster than Data & Analytics in 2025 (8.9% vs 5.0%) and its margin rose to 55.6% [S120]. Confirmed And Markets feeds the data businesses: every trade on LSE, Turquoise or Tradeweb produces prices that are resold. Inferred

Don't say this

"LSEG makes most of its money from the stock exchange." It does not. Data & Analytics alone is about 44% of income, and the equities trading line is £412m out of nearly £9bn [S120]. Say "LSEG is a data and infrastructure group; the London Stock Exchange is the brand people know, not the biggest earner."

MK1056KMHow LSEG differs from a bank, an asset manager and Bloomberg

Interviewers often test whether you understand what LSEG is not. Use these three contrasts.

Compared withWhat they doWhat LSEG does insteadThe one-line difference
A bankLends, takes deposits and trades with its own balance sheet. It can lose money on positions.Runs the venues and data that banks use. LCH manages default risk, but as a risk mutualiser funded by members' margin and default fund, not as a lender.Banks take market risk; LSEG charges a toll on the road they drive on. Inferred
An asset managerInvests clients' money and earns a fee on assets under management.FTSE Russell licenses the index that passive funds track and sells them data, but does not manage the money.The asset manager runs the fund; LSEG sells it the recipe. Inferred
BloombergA private company built around its terminal and news; also runs FXGO and bond trading.Listed on the LSE, and combines data with regulated market infrastructure (venues and clearing). Bloomberg and LSEG are the two largest market data vendors, followed by S&P Global [S188, S189].Bloomberg owns the screen; LSEG owns the screen and the plumbing. Inferred
Source uncertain

The vendor ranking (Bloomberg first, LSEG second, S&P third) comes from Burton-Taylor headlines based on 2023 data [S189]; the 2025 report confirms total spend of $49.2bn but its market shares are paywalled [S188]. Say "one of the two largest", not a percentage.

MK1057KMThe structural forces reshaping FMI now

Ten forces explain almost every headline about LSEG. The figure that follows groups the eight with clearest money effects into a single map; the table gives all ten with the evidence.

#ForceEvidenceWhat it means for LSEG
1Shift to data and subscriptionsGlobal market data spend up 6.5% to a record $49.2bn in 2025 [S188], from $42bn in 2023, when Burton-Taylor said AI had "elevated the value of market data" [S189]. ConfirmedSupports D&A and FTSE Russell, which are c.55% of income [S120]. Inferred
2Electronification of bonds and FXAbout 44% of US investment-grade corporate bond volume was electronic in 2024; Tradeweb about 34% share vs MarketAxess 37% [S190]. Reported FX spot rose to 31% of turnover in 2025 from 28% [S163].Tradeweb grew revenue 18.9% in 2025 [S137]; LSEG FX average daily volume $525bn in 2025 [S120].
3AI as threat and opportunityOliver Wyman: AI threatens about $12bn (9%) of FMI revenue, creates about $9bn new, and offers over 20% cost reduction [S185]."LSEG Everywhere": AI-ready data via MCP, Amazon Quick and Google Gemini partnerships; 17,000 active AI Search users in Workspace [S195].
4Cloud and concentration riskUK critical third parties (CTP) regime from 1 Jan 2025; first designations 13 Jul 2026 [S170]: AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft, Oracle [S171]. ReportedLSEG's 10-year Microsoft partnership (Dec 2022) includes $2.8bn minimum cloud spend [S147].
5Tokenisation and digital assetsDigital Securities Sandbox in force 8 Jan 2024, opened 30 Sep 2024 [S169, S168]. BoE consulting on tokenised assets as CCP collateral [S184].LSEG's "Digital Securities Depository collaboration with HSBC on DIGIT" [S195].
6Private markets growthPISCES lets private company shares trade at set events [S152]. Mansion House Accord (13 May 2025): 10% of default funds in private markets by 2030, half in the UK [S181]. ReportedLSE Private Securities Market held its first auction on 25 Mar 2026 [S154]. Reported
7Passive investing and indexingMoney moving to index funds benefits index providers. Inferred No sourced share figure in our research.FTSE Russell £954m [S120].
8Clearing mandates and geopoliticsEMIR 3 forces some EU firms to hold an active account at an EU CCP from 25 Jun 2025 [S161]; EU equivalence for UK CCPs extended to 30 Jun 2028 [S160].Direct threat to LCH euro swaps; Eurex rose to 13.5% of EUR swaps in Q3 2025 from 8.4% [S139]. Reported
9Buy-side pressure on data feesFCA wholesale data study (29 Feb 2024): users "may be paying higher prices ... than if competition was working more effectively", but no significant intervention [S165].Pricing scrutiny on D&A and venue data; the risk is regulatory, not just commercial. Inferred
10Consolidated tapesUK bond tape live 22 Jun 2026 [S155]; equity tape procurement early 2027, live "in 2027 or early 2028" [S157].A cheaper public source of some trade data: a mild threat to venue data income, offset by an income share for contributors. Inferred
Key term

Tokenisation: representing a security or asset as a digital token on a shared ledger (DLT, distributed ledger technology). The promise is faster settlement and easier movement of collateral. The threat to incumbents is that token-native systems could bypass today's post-trade chain. The Bank of England's line: "Real-time payments, electronic securities settlement and central clearing were once novel concepts. Today, they are foundational to the functioning of the financial system" [S184].

Key term

Consolidated tape (CT): one feed combining trade data from every venue for an asset class, so users do not have to buy data from each venue separately. The UK bond tape is run by ETS Connect UK [S155].

MK1058KMWhere the industry goes in three to five years

There is no single consensus. Five credible sources point in four directions. You need to know each, and then pick a position.

ViewWho says itThe numbersWhat would prove it right
1. Steady compounding: data and AI winnersOliver Wyman base case (Jun 2026)FMI revenue grows about 8% a year to around $200bn by 2030 (bull case $230bn). Fastest growth in listed derivatives, commodities and digital assets. Winners focus on defensible cores after $88bn of data and tech acquisitions [S185] ($88bn Reported).Subscription growth keeps accelerating; margins rise. OW says AI cost savings "could lift sector EBITDA margins from 52-54% to more than 60%" [S185].
2. Disintermediation by AI and tokensOliver Wyman headwinds case; Morgan Stanley with Oliver WymanGrowth slows to about 6% a year in an AI-headwinds case; tokenisation could shift 35% of current revenue (about $45bn) to token-native infrastructure [S185]. Tokenised real-world assets $2.3tn by 2030, mostly collateral mobility [S191]. ReportedBig asset managers settle tokenised funds outside CSDs; AI agents replace screens for routine analytics.
3. Non-banks and regulators reshape the client baseBCG (Oct 2025); FCA; EUNon-banks take about 20% of corporate and investment banking revenue and 30% of trading volumes by 2030 [S186]. Regulators push down data costs (FCA study, tapes) [S165, S157] and the EU pulls euro clearing from London [S160]. InferredProp traders become top venue clients; EMIR 3 shifts measurable euro swap share to Eurex.
4. Modernise with Big Tech as partner or rivalMcKinseyThe industry is "thriving" but disruption forces strategic change, with Big Tech partnering incumbents [S187]. ReportedMore cloud co-development deals like LSEG with Microsoft [S147].
Regulator's frame: adopt, but build trustBank of England (Oct 2025)Technology can be adopted, but trust must be built; BoE consulting on tokenised CCP collateral [S184]. Its Omnibus Account (2021) already "supports the settlement of tokenised assets backed in central bank money" [S184].DSS entities go live; tokenised collateral accepted at CCPs.
Source uncertain

Oliver Wyman's report was read through a summariser, and the $88bn figure came from a snippet [S185]. The McKinsey report returned an error and was not read; only its headline framing is known [S187]. The Morgan Stanley figure is from press coverage [S191]. Quote these as "Oliver Wyman estimates" or "McKinsey has argued", never as facts.

The connecting thread. The views are not mutually exclusive. LSEG's own bets are a hedge across all of them: Workspace AI and "LSEG Everywhere" (view 1 and 4), the DIGIT collaboration with HSBC (view 2), LSE 24 and the Private Securities Market (view 3, courting new client types and private capital) [S195, S196]. Inferred

Your opinion goes here

Prompt: "Where do you see our industry in five years?"

Side A (optimist): Oliver Wyman's base case of about 8% a year to around $200bn by 2030 [S185], record data spend [S188] and accelerating subscriptions at LSEG [S195] say the incumbents keep compounding. Network effects in clearing (LCH has 99.995% of GBP SONIA swaps [S140]) are very hard to break.

Side B (disruption): Up to $45bn of revenue could move to token-native rails [S185]; about $12bn is exposed to AI [S185]; regulators are actively pushing data prices down [S165]; the EU is pulling clearing away [S160]. LSEG shares once fell 13% in a single day on AI fears [S146] Reported, so investors take the threat seriously.

Suggested position: "I think the core plumbing (clearing, venues, benchmarks) gets more valuable, not less, because AI and tokens both need trusted data and trusted settlement. The pressure falls on undifferentiated analytics and on per-unit data pricing. The winners will be groups that turn their data into something AI can use and that own the post-trade rails tokenised assets will need. The signals I would watch are PvP adoption in FX, DSS firms going live, take-up of the tapes, and whether EMIR 3 moves real euro swap share." Inferred

Say this in the interview

"Oliver Wyman says data and technology have gone from 21% to 30% of FMI revenue in five years. That is the shift in one number, and LSEG is ahead of it because about 61% of its income is already subscription-based." [S185, S120]

MK1059KMPart 5 in ten lines

  1. FMI is the plumbing: venues, clearing houses, depositories, repositories, plus index and data businesses.
  2. LSEG does five of these jobs at once: exchange, MTF, CCP, index provider, data vendor. Inferred
  3. The lifecycle: pre-trade data, execution, clearing, settlement, post-trade. LSEG is at four of five; not UK settlement. Inferred
  4. Primary market raises money; secondary market trades it afterwards.
  5. Shares trade on lit order books; bonds, swaps and FX mostly by RFQ or OTC. Tradeweb's £1,539m dwarfs Equities' £412m [S120].
  6. Five revenue lines: trading, clearing, listing, data, index. Data & Analytics is the largest at £3,978m [S120].
  7. LSEG is not a bank (no proprietary risk), not an asset manager (no client money), and not Bloomberg (it owns venues and a CCP). Inferred
  8. Market data spend was a record $49.2bn in 2025 [S188]; data and tech are 30% of FMI revenue [S185].
  9. Forces: electronification, AI, cloud concentration, tokens, private markets, EU clearing politics, data price regulation, consolidated tapes.
  10. Have a view: core plumbing gets more valuable; generic analytics and per-unit data pricing face pressure. Inferred

The role's own industry and its regulation

The four markets an intern could land in, how they got here, the rules being rewritten around them right now, and the one sentence to say about each rule.

Almost every rule below has a date between mid-2024 and late 2027, which is exactly when you would intern (June 2027) and graduate (summer 2028). Inferred

MK1061KMHow we got here: the history in six steps

DateEventWhat happenedWhy it still matters
Jul 1963First Eurobond (Autostrade)$15m, 15 years, 5.5% coupon, lead-managed from London by S G Warburg [S174]. Confirmed Listed in Luxembourg, not London [S175]. ReportedThe origin of London as a centre for international debt, the heritage behind ISM and the debt listings team.
27 Oct 1986"Big Bang"Fixed commissions scrapped, foreign firms allowed to buy UK brokers, firms allowed to be both broker and dealer, floor trading replaced by screens [S178]. ReportedCreated the modern electronic, international LSE.
1 Nov 2007MiFID (EU)EU rules allowed exchanges and MTFs to compete for trading [S203].How Turquoise and Chi-X emerged: venue competition is why the LSE no longer has all UK share trading. Inferred
3 Jan 2018MiFID II / MiFIRMore transparency, research unbundling, share and derivatives trading obligations, more reporting [S203]. ReportedBuilt today's reporting and data rules; much of the UK rewrite since 2023 is adjusting it.
Jan 2021Brexit, end of transitionEU share trading moved from London to Amsterdam. Amsterdam averaged €9.2bn a day in January 2021 vs London €8.6bn [S179]. ReportedLost EU share volumes; the reason the UK started to rewrite its own rules.
2023 to 2026The UK rebuildSTO scrapped (29 Aug 2023), Listing Rules rewritten (29 Jul 2024), PISCES (Jun 2025), prospectus regime replaced (19 Jan 2026), bond tape live (22 Jun 2026), T+1 planned (11 Oct 2027) [S167, S150, S152, S151, S155, S158].The live agenda you are being hired into.
Don't say this

"The first Eurobond was listed in London in 1963." It was arranged in London by S G Warburg, but listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange [S174, S175]. Say: "The Eurobond market was born in London in 1963 with the Autostrade deal, led by Warburg, even though the bond itself was listed in Luxembourg." Getting this detail right is exactly the kind of care a debt listings team notices.

Key term

Eurobond: a bond issued in a currency other than that of the country where it is issued, sold to international investors. ICMA: "It is generally accepted that the Eurobond market began with the Autostrade issue for the Italian motorway network in July 1963" [S174].

Key term

MiFID / MiFID II / MiFIR: EU rules on investment services and trading venues. After Brexit the UK kept its own amended version, "UK MiFIR", which it is now changing piece by piece. FSMA 2023 (the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023) is the law that lets it do so.

MK1062KMPrimary markets and debt listings

This is the London Stock Exchange's home turf: helping companies and governments raise money. The equity side has had a hard decade; the debt side is quieter but steady. Since 2024 the government and FCA have changed nearly every rule an issuer touches. Inferred

Key term

IPO (initial public offering): a company's first sale of shares to the public, with admission to trading. Prospectus: the legal document describing the security and the issuer, so investors can judge it.

Key term

Listing vs admission to trading: "listing" means joining an official list with its rules; "admission to trading" means the venue lets the security trade. On a regulated market you usually need both; on an MTF like AIM or ISM the exchange alone admits. Inferred

UK Listing Rules (UKLR)Listings
When FCA PS24/6 published 11 Jul 2024; rules in force 29 Jul 2024 [S150]
What Scraps the old "premium" and "standard" listing segments "in favour of a new commercial companies category for equity shares" [S150], commonly called ESCC (equity shares in commercial companies) Reported. Fewer hurdles: for example, no mandatory shareholder votes on most large deals and easier dual-class share structures [S202] Reported. The FCA called it "the most significant changes to the UK's listing regime in over 3 decades" [S150].
Why LSEG Lowers the cost and friction of listing in London, so the LSE can win IPOs back from New York and Amsterdam. EY says "recent reforms to the UK's listing regime are beginning to have a tangible impact" [S142].
Say "Since July 2024 London has one main listing category instead of two, which removes a big reason founders chose New York."
POATRs: the new prospectus regimeListings
When Public Offers and Admissions to Trading Regulations 2024; FCA rules PS25/9 (and PS25/10 for public offer platforms), both 15 Jul 2025; in force 19 Jan 2026 [S151]
What Replaces the UK Prospectus Regulation inherited from the EU. PS25/9 creates a new FCA sourcebook, the Prospectus Rules: Admissions to Trading on Regulated Markets (PRM) [S151].
Why LSEG Changes the cost of raising money on the Main Market, for both shares and bonds, because the prospectus is one of the most expensive parts of a listing. Inferred The JD's "debt listings" research sits right on top of this.
Say "Since 19 January 2026 prospectuses for London's regulated markets sit under the FCA's new PRM rules, so the question for the debt listings team is whether that makes the Main Market more competitive with MTF routes like ISM."
Source uncertain

Detailed POATRs thresholds (for example a 75% limit for further share issues without a prospectus, or protected forward-looking statements) and the SI number were not on the FCA page read for this pack. Do not quote them. If asked, say you know the regime went live on 19 January 2026 under PS25/9 and that you would want to check the thresholds.

PISCES and LSE's Private Securities MarketListings
When Sandbox regulations laid 15 May 2025, in force 5 Jun 2025; FCA PS25/6 rules in force 10 Jun 2025; sandbox ends 5 Jun 2030 unless extended [S152]
What "PISCES is a new type of share trading platform. It allows buyers and sellers of shares in private companies to trade those shares during intermittent trading periods" [S152]. It is secondary trading only: no new money is raised [S154] Reported.
Why LSEG LSE's PISCES venue is the Private Securities Market (PSM). FCA approval reported 26 Aug 2025 [S153] Reported; rules published 5 Feb 2026; first auction 25 Mar 2026, for a Tradeable Private Equity Investment Company holding shares in Oxford Science Enterprises [S154] Reported. LSEG's H1 2026 results cite "first Private Securities Markets transactions" [S195] Confirmed. A new product line and a possible pipeline to the Main Market. Inferred
Say "PSM lets private companies get used to a London trading venue before they IPO; I would track how many PSM companies later move to the Main Market."
UK Listing Relief (stamp duty)Listings
When Autumn Budget 26 Nov 2025; applies to shares newly listed on a UK regulated market on or after 27 Nov 2025 [S182]
What A three-year relief from the 0.5% stamp duty reserve tax (SDRT) on buying shares in newly listed companies [S182] Reported. EY also refers to "the newly announced UK Listing Relief" [S192].
Why LSEG Makes newly listed UK shares cheaper to buy, which helps IPO demand. Only applies to regulated markets, so it favours the Main Market over AIM. Inferred
Say "For three years, investors buying a new London listing pay no stamp duty: a direct nudge towards the Main Market."
Pension and savings reforms: Mansion House, Leeds, ISAsListings
When Edinburgh Reforms 9 Dec 2022 [S199]; Mansion House Compact 10 Jul 2023; Mansion House Accord 13 May 2025 [S181]; Leeds Reforms 15 Jul 2025 [S180]; cash ISA limit cut from 6 Apr 2027 [S183]
What Compact: nine DC pension providers aim for at least 5% of default funds in unlisted equities by 2030. Accord: 17 signatories, at least 10% of main default funds in private markets by 2030, half in the UK [S181] Reported. Leeds Reforms aim to make the UK the number one destination for financial services by 2035 [S180] Reported. Cash ISA limit falls to £12,000 (overall £20,000 unchanged) to push savers towards shares [S183] Reported.
Why LSEG More domestic money for UK companies, both private (PSM, private markets data) and listed (retail demand). The government is explicitly trying to fix the demand side of the listings problem, not only the rules. Inferred
Say "The reforms attack both sides of the drought: rules for issuers (UKLR, POATRs) and money from pensions and savers (Mansion House, ISAs)."

Debt listings: Main Market, ISM and the Sustainable Bond Market

The JD singles out "debt listings". This is less glamorous than IPOs but London has deep roots in it, going back to the 1963 Eurobond. LSE offers two main routes and one label on top. Inferred

  • Main Market: the regulated market, used for debt listings including gilts and sovereign bonds Inferred. Prospectuses now fall under the FCA's PRM rules [S151].
  • International Securities Market (ISM): an MTF for debt sold to professional investors; launched 8 May 2017 with first admissions on 15 May 2017; admission is approved by LSE, not via the FCA's Official List [S176] Reported.
  • Sustainable Bond Market: launched 11 Oct 2019, building on the Green Bond Segment from 2015. LSE says it "was the first major exchange to launch a dedicated Green Bond Segment" [S177] Confirmed.
Key term

Professional investors: banks, fund managers, insurers and other institutions treated as able to look after themselves, so the rules for selling to them are lighter than for retail savers. ISM is built for them, which is why it can be quicker and simpler than a regulated market listing. Inferred

Source uncertain

Our research does not contain ISM or Main Market fees, timetables, minimum denominations, the number of bonds listed, or LSEG's debt listings revenue. Figure 30 therefore keeps those steps generic. If the debt listings team comes up, ask about these rather than guess: "How do issuers choose between ISM and the Main Market today?" is a strong question.

MK1063KMEquities trading, transparency and market data

Share trading in London is split across the LSE order book, MTFs like Turquoise and Cboe Europe, dark books and bank systematic internalisers. The rules here decide where trades can happen and who owns the data they produce. Inferred

Key term

Systematic internaliser (SI): a bank or firm that trades against its own book with clients on an organised, frequent basis. It competes with venues for the same share trades. Pre-trade transparency means publishing bids and offers before trading; post-trade transparency means publishing the price and size after. A deferral lets a dealer delay publishing a large trade so it can hedge.

Share trading obligation (STO) revokedTrading and data
When 29 Aug 2023, by commencement of FSMA 2023 [S167]
What "On 29 August 2023, the Share Trading Obligation (STO) in Article 23 of UK MiFIR was revoked" [S167]. The STO forced certain share trades onto venues; firms can now trade those shares more freely, including on non-UK venues. Inferred
Why LSEG Removes a Brexit-era friction for UK firms trading EU shares, but also removes a rule that pushed flow onto venues like LSE and Turquoise. Mixed for LSEG. Inferred
Say "The UK dropped the share trading obligation in August 2023, which made London more open, but it means LSE and Turquoise have to win flow on quality, not by rule."
Bond and derivatives transparencyTrading and data
When FCA PS24/14, published 5 Nov 2024; rules in force 1 Dec 2025 [S156]
What "A simpler and more timely post-trade transparency regime based on fewer deferrals" for bonds and derivatives [S156].
Why LSEG More bond trade data published faster: good for price discovery, and the foundation for the bond consolidated tape. Tradeweb is a bond venue that publishes data under these rules. Inferred
Say "PS24/14 is the bond transparency rulebook; it is not the tape itself, it is the data the tape is built from."
UK bond consolidated tapeTrading and data
When FCA authorised ETS Connect UK (Etrading Software) in May 2026; "launched the UK bond CT service on 22 June 2026"; 5-year term [S155]
What One feed combining bond trade reports from all UK venues. The contract value of about £4.8m and a High Court case that delayed the award (lifted Dec 2025) come from press snippets only [S155] Reported.
Why LSEG Gives bond investors a cheap consolidated view of trades. A mild competitive threat to venue data sales, and a reason for Tradeweb and LSEG to sell richer data on top. Inferred
Say "The UK bond tape went live on 22 June 2026, run by ETS Connect UK, not by LSEG, so LSEG's data value has to come from analytics, not raw trade prints."
UK equity consolidated tapeTrading and data
When FCA CP26/31 (policy statement plus consultation), first published 19 Nov 2025, updated 31 Jul 2026; procurement early 2027; operating "in 2027 or early 2028" [S157]
What The equity tape will include post-trade data plus "the first level of pre-trade data (the attributed best bid and offer)". The tape provider (CTP) must share income with data contributors [S157].
Why LSEG LSE and Turquoise will be contributors and may get an income share, but the tape also offers a cheaper alternative to buying each venue's data. Inferred Including pre-trade best bid and offer makes this more powerful than a post-trade-only tape. Inferred
Say "The equity tape includes best bid and offer, not just trades, and it shares revenue with venues, so for LSE it is part threat, part new income line."
FCA wholesale data market studyTrading and data
When Final report and press release, 29 Feb 2024 [S165]
What Found "users may be paying higher prices for the data they buy than if competition was working more effectively", but Sheldon Mills said: "We do not believe the case has been made for significant interventions. However, we will examine ways to help support wholesale data being provided on fair, reasonable and transparent terms" [S165]. A snippet reports operating margins of key wholesale data providers of 30% to 60%+ over 2017 to 2022 [S165] Reported.
Why LSEG LSEG is one of the largest data providers. No big intervention, but the regulator is watching pricing, and the tapes are partly a response. Inferred
Say "The FCA looked hard at data pricing in 2024 and stopped short of intervening; LSEG's licence to price data is earned, not guaranteed."
UK MAR and market cleanlinessTrading and data
When UK Market Abuse Regulation; FCA market cleanliness statistic 2025: 41.1% [S166]
What UK MAR bans insider dealing, unlawful disclosure of inside information and market manipulation; issuers must disclose inside information promptly and keep insider lists Inferred. The FCA's market cleanliness statistic (share of takeovers with abnormal share price moves before the announcement) was 41.1% in 2025; the 5-year average is 33.74% [S166]. The FCA says the revised method gives "systematically higher" figures [S166].
Why LSEG Venue operators must monitor for abuse. A rising cleanliness number is a reputational issue for London as a market. Inferred It also connects directly to LSEG's value of Integrity.
Say "The 2025 market cleanliness figure was 41.1%, but the FCA changed its method, so I would not read it as a sudden jump without checking the footnote."
Key term

Inside information: precise, non-public information that would move a security's price if known. Insider list: the record an issuer keeps of everyone with access to it.

LSEG's own move: LSE 24. Announced 21 July 2026, LSE 24 is a separate venue trading 24 hours a day, five days a week. It "will be available for client testing by the end of 2026, with Exchange Traded Products (ETPs) launching as the first asset class in H1 2027, subject to regulatory approval" [S196]. Confirmed It will mix order book and RFQ functionality [S196]. This is not a regulation, but it lands in the middle of the regulatory timeline and answers the retail demand that the ISA changes are trying to create. Inferred

MK1064KMFX electronic trading

FX is the largest market in the world, and London is its centre. LSEG FX runs FXall, where banks trade with clients (dealer-to-client, D2C), and FX Matching, where banks trade with each other (dealer-to-dealer, D2D), with LCH ForexClear clearing some FX derivatives [S120].

$9.6tn
Global FX turnover a day, Apr 2025, up 28% from $7.5tn in 2022 [S163]
37.8%
UK share of global FX ($4,745bn a day), down from 38.0% [S162]
89.2%
Share of FX trades with the US dollar on one side [S163]
$1.4tn
FX settled each day with no protection, about 10% [S205]

Other facts worth holding: spot is 31% of turnover and FX swaps 42%; the top four centres (UK, US, Singapore, Hong Kong) account for 75% [S163]. The UK is also 49.6% of global OTC interest rate derivatives turnover [S162]. Confirmed The Bank of England: "The UK remains the single largest centre of foreign exchange activity with share of 37.8% of global turnover" [S162].

Key term

Spot FX: exchanging currencies for near-immediate delivery (usually two days). FX swap: a spot trade plus a reverse forward trade, used by banks and corporates to manage funding. Swaps are the biggest single product at 42% of turnover [S163].

Key term

D2C and D2D: dealer-to-client platforms (FXall) let corporates and asset managers request prices from several banks. Dealer-to-dealer platforms (FX Matching) let banks trade with each other, usually on an order book. LSEG runs both.

FX Global Code: 2024 reviewFX
When GFXC three-year review completed 10 Dec 2024; updated Code published Jan 2025 [S164]
What A voluntary set of 55 principles of good practice for the FX market, written by the Global Foreign Exchange Committee (GFXC) and first published in 2017 [S204] Reported. The 2024 review aimed "to strengthen the Code's guidance on FX settlement risk and to increase transparency around certain types of FX transactions and the use of client-generated data" [S164].
Why LSEG FXall's clients (banks, corporates, asset managers) sign statements of commitment to the Code. Questions about how platforms use client data and how settlement risk is reduced are live client topics an FX intern would hear. Inferred
Say "The FX Global Code was updated in December 2024 to tighten guidance on settlement risk and on how client data is used, which is exactly what a platform like FXall has to answer to."
FX settlement risk: the BIS measurementFX
When BIS Quarterly Review, 15 Jun 2026, based on the April 2025 Triennial Survey [S205]
What "Just over one third of the average daily settlement volume in April 2025, or $5.2 trillion, was settled via PvP, which eliminates settlement risk" [S205]. About 10%, or $1.4tn a day, settled with no protection at all [S205]. CLS has offered PvP since September 2002 [S204] Reported.
Why LSEG Settlement risk is the biggest unsolved problem in FX. Any LSEG FX workflow that helps clients route more trades into PvP or clearing (ForexClear) answers a regulator-backed need. Inferred
Say "BIS found about $1.4 trillion of FX a day still settles with no protection, so post-trade is where FX innovation will be judged."

LSEG FX in numbers. Average daily total volume $525bn in 2025, up 9.6%; ForexClear notional cleared $48,113bn, up 31.4% [S120]. Confirmed H1 2025 average daily volume was $530bn, up 14.2% [S198] Reported, and ForexClear was reported up 45% in H1 2026 [S198, S195] Reported. Note the different periods before comparing them.

MK1065KMClearing and settlement

LCH is LSEG's most strategically valuable asset and its most politically exposed. It dominates swap clearing in most currencies, and the EU wants a bigger share of euro clearing at home. Inferred

$1,941tn
SwapClear IRS notional cleared 2025, +21.2% [S120]
86.5%
LCH share of EUR swaps Q3 2025; Eurex 13.5% (from 8.4%) [S139]
99.995%

94.2%

EMIR 3 and the active account requirementClearing
When EU; in force 24 Dec 2024; active account requirement applies from 25 Jun 2025 [S161]
What Some EU firms must hold an "active account" at an EU CCP and clear part of their euro and Polish zloty interest rate derivatives and euro short-term interest rate derivatives through it: at least five trades per sub-category per reference period [S161] Reported.
Why LSEG A direct attempt to move euro swap clearing from LCH to EU CCPs such as Eurex. Eurex's share of EUR swaps rose from 8.4% to 13.5% in a year to Q3 2025 [S139] Reported. LCH's defence is netting: splitting a portfolio across two CCPs raises margin for the user. Inferred
Say "EMIR 3's active accounts went live in June 2025; the test is whether euro swap share keeps moving to Eurex or whether the cost of splitting netting sets keeps users at LCH."
EU equivalence for UK CCPsClearing
When European Commission decision 31 Jan 2025; three-year extension to 30 Jun 2028, applying from 1 Jul 2025 [S160]
What Lets EU firms keep using UK CCPs like LCH. Commissioner Albuquerque: "With this extension of equivalence for UK CCPs we are safeguarding EU financial stability and avoiding short-term risks", and the extension "will allow the recently agreed EMIR 3 measures to start taking effect, increasing clearing in the EU and reducing our exposure to UK CCPs" [S160].
Why LSEG The single most important date for LCH. Without renewal, EU members could face limits on using LCH after 30 Jun 2028. Inferred
Say "EU equivalence for LCH runs to 30 June 2028; that is the cliff edge, and the EU said openly it is buying time for EMIR 3 to pull clearing home."
UK CCP rules move to the Bank of EnglandClearing
When FSMA 2023 rule-making powers; BoE consultation Jul 2025 on an FMI Rulebook; final rules no earlier than mid-2026 [S197]
What The Bank of England gains powers to write its own rules for CCPs and CSDs, replacing retained EU law (UK EMIR) [S197] Reported. Separately, it is "consulting ... on ... permitting tokenised assets as eligible collateral for CCPs" [S184].
Why LSEG LCH Ltd's UK rulebook will be rewritten by its home regulator, and tokenised collateral could change what members post as margin. Inferred
Say "LCH's rulebook is moving from retained EU law to a Bank of England FMI Rulebook, and the Bank is even consulting on tokenised collateral."
Source uncertain

Whether the Bank of England's final CCP rules were published in 2026 is not known from our research [S197]. The EMIR 3 legal citation is also unverified. Say "the Bank consulted in July 2025" rather than "the new rules are in force".

T+1 settlementClearing
When UK draft SI, "The Central Securities Depositories (Amendment) (Intended Settlement Date) Regulations 2026", published 20 Nov 2025, comments to 27 Feb 2026; T+1 "from 11 October 2027" [S158]. EU Regulation (EU) 2025/2075, OJ 14 Oct 2025, applies from 11 Oct 2027 [S159]
What Trades in shares and bonds must settle one business day after the trade, not two. UK and EU move on the same day, so cross-border trades stay aligned [S158, S159].
Why LSEG Less time to fix errors means more automation and same-day trade checks; less counterparty risk; LCH and venue operations must adapt. Risk teams will watch settlement fails. Inferred It lands four months after a June 2027 internship starts.
Say "T+1 arrives on 11 October 2027 in both the UK and EU, which halves the time to fix a broken trade, so operations and risk teams will be judged on automation."
Source uncertain: T+1 legal status

Only the draft UK statutory instrument (November 2025) is confirmed [S158]. Whether the final SI has been made in 2026 is not verified. Say "the UK has legislated in draft for T+1 on 11 October 2027, the same day as the EU", not "the law is in force". The EU regulation is published [S159] but was read via a secondary source.

The commercial backdrop. In 2025 LSEG paid £1.2bn to cut the founding banks' share of SwapClear's revenue surplus from c.30% to 15% for 2025 and 10% from 2026 to 2045 [S120]. Confirmed LSEG's H1 2026 margin improved partly due to "the change in the SwapClear revenue share agreement in H2 2025" [S195]. A record $502tn of notional was cleared in Q3 2025 [S198] Reported.

Key term

Vertical silo vs open access: a vertical silo owns trading and clearing for its products and keeps them together (Deutsche Börse describes its "vertically integrated business model" [S127]). Open access means a CCP clears trades from many venues. LCH is the open-access model, partly owned with banks; Euronext pulling its clearing in-house is the silo model winning one round [S120].

The story has turned from "London is dying" to "London is recovering from a low base". Source uncertain

Two research files describe the 88 departures differently: "left the LSE" [S200] and "left the main market" [S145], both citing EY. Say "88 companies left in 2024". The H1 2026 figures are Confirmed in one file [S143] and Reported in the other [S193]; both give 7 listings and £577m.

Your opinion goes here

Prompt: "Is London's listings market fixed?"

Side A (yes, turning): the rules are rewritten (UKLR, POATRs), the tax nudge is in place (UK Listing Relief), pension money is being pointed at UK assets (Mansion House), and 2025 proceeds rose 170% [S150, S151, S182, S181, S142].

Side B (not yet): volumes are tiny next to Hong Kong and New York, 88 companies left in 2024, and big names like Visma keep postponing [S134, S145, S194].

Suggested position: "The supply-side rules are mostly fixed; the demand side, meaning domestic pension and retail money, is the slower fix. I would judge it by 2027 and 2028 Main Market IPO counts, and by whether PSM companies graduate to the Main Market." Inferred

2. Other live issues

  • Euro clearing politics. EMIR 3 active accounts and the 30 Jun 2028 equivalence date [S161, S160].
  • Data pricing and AI. The FCA's view on data prices [S165], plus investor worry that AI erodes data businesses: LSEG shares fell 13% in one day on AI fears and were still 23% below their 2025 peak in June 2026 [S146] Reported.
  • T+1 readiness for 11 Oct 2027 [S158], and FX settlement risk of $1.4tn a day [S205].
  • New hours and new markets. LSE 24 (ETPs from H1 2027, subject to approval) and PSM [S196, S154].

MK1007KM
Part 7

What is happening right now

Fifteen stories from the last ten months, what each one means for LSEG and for your seat, and the dates that will move before your interview.

This part is your commercial awareness file. Interviewers on the Markets side expect you to know what their business did this year, not just what LSEG is. Every story below follows the same pattern: what happened, why LSEG cares, which of the four internship duty areas it touches, and a question or opinion you can use. The four duty areas come straight from the job description [JD]:

FX customers solving problems for LSEG FX clients. Markets research research into global markets, including debt listings, valuations, shareholder and geographic analysis. BI and strategy business intelligence, strategic initiatives and operational improvement. Risk monitoring and analysing risks and preparing data for risk projects and reporting.

How to use this part

Do not try to memorise all fifteen stories. Pick three you find genuinely interesting, one of them from the Markets division, and learn them well enough to explain in 60 seconds and give an opinion on. Use the rest as background so that nothing an interviewer mentions surprises you. Re-read the "Diary of dates" table the night before any stage, because some of these stories will have moved on.
